q: According to RFC 9110, which methods are idempotent?
options: GET and POST, because both are the most common methods
Only the safe methods: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE
PUT, DELETE and the safe methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE)
Every method except PATCH, which RFC 5789 excludes
explain: RFC 9110 §9.2.2: "PUT, DELETE, and safe request methods are idempotent." The tempting answer "every method except PATCH" forgets POST, which is neither safe nor idempotent; that is why POST /orders needs an idempotency key to be retried.

q: An order resource has status, shippingAddress and note. The app sends PUT /orders/ord_42 with only { "note": "leave at door" }. What does that request mean?
options: Replace the whole order with this body, so the omitted fields are reset or removed
Change the note and keep the other fields, exactly like a PATCH
Nothing: PUT can only create resources, so the server must answer 405
Append the note to the order history, because PUT is not idempotent
explain: PUT sends the complete new state of the resource at that URL; what you omit is not kept. Treating it like PATCH is the tempting misreading: to change one field, send PATCH with a JSON Merge Patch body (RFC 7396). PUT is idempotent, and it can create or replace.

q: A customer with a valid access token calls DELETE /products/prd_3, a route reserved for back-office staff. Which status fits?
options: 401 Unauthorized, with a WWW-Authenticate header
403 Forbidden: the caller is known but not allowed
400 Bad Request, because the request should not have been sent
409 Conflict, because the role conflicts with the operation
explain: The credentials are valid, so authentication succeeded; the refusal is about permission, which is 403. 401 is for missing or invalid credentials, and RFC 9110 requires it to carry a WWW-Authenticate challenge so the client can authenticate; sending 401 here would make the app log in again for nothing.

q: Customer A requests GET /orders/ord_99, which belongs to customer B. Which response does RFC 9110 explicitly allow in order not to reveal that the order exists?
options: 401 Unauthorized, so the client tries other credentials
200 with an empty object, so the client sees nothing
403 Forbidden, with a detail explaining the order belongs to someone else
404 Not Found, as if the order did not exist
explain: RFC 9110 §15.5.4 says a server that wishes to hide the existence of a forbidden resource MAY respond with 404. A 403 would confirm that ord_99 exists, which leaks information about other customers. A 200 with an empty body hides the error from every generic tool.

q: In an RFC 9457 problem, which member should the app's code use to decide how to react?
options: type, the URI that identifies the kind of problem
title, the short summary of the problem type
detail, the explanation of this occurrence
instance, the URI of this occurrence
explain: RFC 9457 says consumers MUST use the type URI as the primary identifier of the problem. detail is for humans and clients SHOULD NOT parse it; title is advisory text that may be localised. Machine-readable data goes in extension members.

q: An API answers HTTP 200 with the body {"type":"about:blank","title":"Not Found","status":404}. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: the status member in the body is what clients read
The type must be a real URL, never about:blank
The response line must carry the same status as the body; generic software only sees the 200
Problem bodies are only allowed with 5xx status codes
explain: RFC 9457: "Generators MUST use the same status code in the actual HTTP response." Caches, retry logic and monitoring never read the body, so they treat this failure as a success. about:blank is a valid type, and problems are used with any 4xx or 5xx code.

q: The app retries POST /orders with an Idempotency-Key it already used, but with a different amount. What does the IETF Idempotency-Key draft recommend?
options: Replay the response of the first request
422 Unprocessable Content, with a problem body
409 Conflict, as for a request still running
Run the new request and overwrite the stored response
explain: Draft -08 §2.7: reusing a key with a different payload SHOULD get 422. 409 is the answer for a retry while the original is still being processed. Replaying would hide a client bug: the app would believe the second order was created.

q: Orders d, c, b, a, newest first. Page 1 is LIMIT 2 OFFSET 0 and returns [d, c]. A new order e is created, then page 2 is fetched with LIMIT 2 OFFSET 2. What came back (measured on PostgreSQL 18)?
options: [b, a], because the offset ignores new rows
[a], because one row moved to page 1
[e, d], because new rows go to the end
[c, b], so c is shown twice
explain: Measured with PGlite: [c, b]. OFFSET counts rows, so a new row at the top shifts every row down by one and c appears on both pages. The keyset query WHERE (created_at, id) < (c's values) still returned [b, a].

q: The app sends PATCH /orders/ord_42 with If-Match: "3", but the order is now at version 4. What should the server answer?
options: 412 Precondition Failed, and apply nothing
304 Not Modified, because the client has an old copy
409 Conflict after applying the change to version 4
428 Precondition Required, because the ETag is stale
explain: If-Match makes the write conditional: when the condition is false, RFC 9110 has the server answer 412 and not apply the method. 428 (RFC 6585) is for a request that has no precondition at all when one is required; 304 is for conditional reads with If-None-Match.

q: Which change can ship without a new API version, according to GitHub's published list?
options: Renaming the response field total to totalCents
Making the optional currency parameter required
Adding an optional giftMessage field to the order response
Removing an endpoint that the logs show is rarely called
explain: Adding a response field is additive: tolerant readers ignore fields they do not know. Renaming a field, making a parameter required and removing an operation are all in GitHub's breaking list. A rarely called endpoint still has callers: deprecate it with Deprecation and Sunset headers first.

q: The shop will open Orders API v2 to delivery partners, who must build their integrations before the server exists. Which approach fits best?
options: Code-first, generating the document once the server is finished
Design-first: write and review the OpenAPI document with the partners, then implement it
tRPC, so the partners share the server's TypeScript types
No contract document; partners read the generated SDK code
explain: When consumers must agree on the contract before code exists, the document comes first and both sides build from it. Code-first is a good fit when one team owns server and clients, but here it would make partners wait. tRPC only works for TypeScript clients in the same codebase.

q: The POST /webhooks/payments handler sometimes receives the same payment.succeeded event twice. What should it do?
options: Answer 409 the second time so the sender stops retrying
Process each delivery: senders guarantee each event arrives once
Compare the event timestamps and keep the most recent one
Store each processed event id with a unique constraint and skip duplicates
explain: Retries make duplicates normal; Stripe documents that endpoints may receive the same event more than once and that order is not guaranteed. So the receiver deduplicates on the event id (webhook-id in Standard Webhooks). Answering 409 is a non-2xx response, so the sender would keep retrying it.

q: Customer support emails contain links like https://api.example.com/orders/ord_42/cancel?token=… handled by a GET route. After a chat tool started showing link previews, orders get cancelled on their own. Which fix would you ship?
options: Make the link open a page whose button sends POST /orders/ord_42/cancellation
Keep GET but block the preview bot's user agent
Keep GET but require a second token in the query string
Return 202 Accepted instead of 200 from the GET route
explain: GET is safe by definition, so crawlers and link previewers call it freely; RFC 9110 says a resource MUST disallow an unsafe action when it is accessed with a safe method. Blocking one user agent fixes this bot and not the next one; the state change must move behind POST.

q: An order search takes nested filters too large for a URL. Which statement is accurate as of 2026?
options: Send GET with a JSON body: Node's fetch supports it and caches handle it
Use QUERY (RFC 10008), safe and idempotent with a body, if the whole path supports it; otherwise a documented POST /orders/search
Use PUT /orders/search, because PUT is idempotent and accepts a body
Split the filters across several GET requests and merge the results on the client
explain: RFC 10008 (June 2026) defines QUERY as safe and idempotent with a request body; Fastify 5.12.7 routed it natively in our test. GET with a body is not an option: measured, Node's fetch throws "Request with GET/HEAD method cannot have body." PUT means "replace the resource at this URL", which a search is not.

q: What is the production problem with this v1 handler?
options: The 201 should be a 200, because the order is not paid yet
reply.send without await leaks the promise and the response is never sent
Failures go out as 200, so alerting, retry logic and error-rate dashboards see successes
The body of an error must be a string, so the object breaks serialization
explain: Without reply.code, Fastify sends 200, so an out-of-stock order is invisible to every tool that reads only the status. The fix is a problem body with the right status, such as 409 or 422 with a documented type. Returning reply.send from an async handler is the correct Fastify pattern.

q: A Fastify 5.12.7 app has only GET /orders. A client sends DELETE /orders. What did it receive (measured)?
options: 405 Method Not Allowed with Allow: GET, HEAD
200 with an empty body, because DELETE is idempotent
501 Not Implemented, because the method is unknown
404 with {"message":"Route DELETE:/orders not found",…}
explain: Measured: Fastify answered 404 with its default JSON body, not the 405 that RFC 9110 describes (a 405 MUST include an Allow header). It is a common interview follow-up: know your framework's defaults, and add 405 handling yourself if your contract promises it.

q: During a database failover, every request to the Orders API fails for about 30 seconds. Which response helps clients most?
options: 429 Too Many Requests with RateLimit headers
503 Service Unavailable with Retry-After: 30
500 Internal Server Error with the database error in detail
200 with a "degraded" flag in the body
explain: RFC 9110 defines 503 for temporary overload or maintenance, and Retry-After tells clients when to come back. 429 means this client exceeded its quota, which is false here and misleads per-client backoff. A 500 tells clients nothing about retrying, and the database error must never reach them.

q: What is the bug in this error handler?
options: For a 500, detail exposes the internal error message (SQL, hostnames) to clients
about:blank cannot be used with a status other than 404
title must be different for each occurrence of the error
statusCode is never set on Fastify errors, so everything becomes a 500
explain: An unexpected error message can contain a SQL statement, a hostname or a secret; a 500 should say only that an unexpected error occurred, with a request id, and log the rest. With about:blank the title should be the status phrase, which this code does correctly. Fastify sets statusCode on its own errors, such as 400 for invalid JSON.

q: An idempotency layer looks up the key, creates the order if the key is unknown, then saves the key with the response. Two retries of POST /orders with the same key arrive 5 ms apart. What happens?
options: The second retry waits on a lock until the first finishes
The database rejects the second order because the key is unique
Both see an unknown key and both create an order; the key must be reserved before the work
The second retry gets 409, because the first one is still running
explain: Check-then-act across an await is a race: nothing marks the key as taken until the end. Reserving first (INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING) gives exactly one owner, and the other request sees an in-progress key and gets 409. The unique key only protects the idempotency table, not the order that was already created twice.

q: This statement returns 0 rows. What should the request do next?
code:
INSERT INTO idempotency_keys (account_id, key, fingerprint)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3)
ON CONFLICT (account_id, key) DO NOTHING
RETURNING key;
options: Run the operation: 0 rows means the insert succeeded silently
Retry the INSERT until it returns 1 row
Answer 500, because the insert failed with a unique violation
Read the existing row: replay if completed, 409 if in progress, 422 if the fingerprint differs
explain: Measured with PGlite: the first insert returned 1 row (this request owns the key) and the second returned 0 rows because the key existed. ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING raises no error; a plain INSERT would have failed with 23505. Zero rows means someone else owns the key, so the request reads it and decides.

q: With Stripe's API v1, a POST with an idempotency key fails parameter validation. The client fixes the body and retries with the same key. What does Stripe document?
options: The retry gets the stored validation error, because the first response is saved
The retry runs: results are saved only once execution begins, and a validation failure saves nothing
The retry gets 422, because the body differs from the first request
The retry gets 409 until the 24-hour expiry has passed
explain: Stripe: "If incoming parameters fail validation … we don't save the idempotent result", so the client can retry. Saving the first response, "including 500 errors", applies only once the endpoint has started executing. The 422-for-a-different-body rule applies to a stored key, and there is none here.

q: Orders o1, o2, o3 share the same created_at; o4 is older. Page 1, sorted by created_at DESC, id DESC with limit 2, returned [o3, o2]. Page 2 uses WHERE created_at < $1 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 2 with o2's timestamp. What did it return (measured)?
options: [o4]: o1 is skipped because it shares the boundary timestamp
[o1, o4]: the database keeps insertion order
[o2, o1]: rows equal to the boundary are included
An error, because the sort has duplicates
explain: Measured with PGlite: [o4]. Strictly less than the timestamp excludes every row with that timestamp, including o1, which was never shown. Comparing the tuple (created_at, id) < (o2's values) returned [o1, o4]: the id tie-breaker makes the order total.

q: A teammate decodes cursors with JSON.parse(Buffer.from(cursor, 'base64url').toString()) and no validation, arguing that Node rejects invalid base64. What is true?
options: They are right: Buffer.from throws on characters outside the base64url alphabet
Validation is useless because cursors are encrypted by base64url
Buffer.from does not throw: '%%%not-base64' decoded to junk bytes, so parse in a try and validate the shape
Cursors should be plain JSON in the query string so that no decoding is needed
explain: Measured on Node 24: Buffer.from('%%%not-base64', 'base64url') returned junk bytes without throwing, and a well-formed cursor can still carry a wrong shape or a fake timestamp. Base64url is an encoding, not encryption. Decode in a try, validate with a schema, answer 400 otherwise, and sign it if tampering matters.

q: What is the concurrency bug in this PATCH handler?
options: If-Match must be compared with weak comparison, so the check always fails
The handler should answer 409, not 412, when versions differ
The version should be incremented by the client, not by SQL
Another request can update the order between the check and the UPDATE; put AND version = $3 in the WHERE
explain: The check and the write are two steps, so two requests with the same ETag can both pass the check and both write: the lost update comes back. Putting the expected version in the UPDATE's WHERE makes the database decide atomically; measured, the stale update returned no row. RFC 9110 requires strong comparison for If-Match, not weak.

q: Several support agents edit the same orders, and some old back-office clients never send If-Match, so they still overwrite changes. What can the server do?
options: Answer 412 to every write so clients reload first
Require the header: answer 428 Precondition Required to writes without If-Match
Answer 304 Not Modified to writes that lack an ETag
Lock the order row for the whole time an agent has it open
explain: RFC 6585 defines 428 exactly for this: the origin server requires the request to be conditional, to avoid lost updates. 412 is for a precondition that was sent and is false. Long-held locks across user think time block other agents and break when a browser tab is closed.

q: The API adds "partially_refunded" to the order status enum, an additive change in GitHub's list. The Android app then crashes on some orders. Why, and what prevents it?
options: Adding enum values is breaking in every API, so a v2 was required
The server should have sent a Sunset header for the old enum
The client switch was exhaustive with no default; document that enums can grow and make clients handle unknown values
JSON cannot carry new string values without a schema change on the client
explain: Additive for the server is not harmless for a strict client: an exhaustive switch or a closed generated enum type fails on a value it does not know. The contract must say enums can grow, and generated clients should keep unknown values. Sunset announces a removal; nothing was removed here.

q: In October 2026, a script calls GitHub's REST API without an X-GitHub-Api-Version header. Which version does it get, according to GitHub's docs?
options: 2022-11-28, the default for requests without the header
2026-03-10, the latest version
An error, because the header is required
Whichever version the token was created with
explain: GitHub documents that requests without the header use 2022-11-28, although 2026-03-10 is the latest version, and that versions stay supported for 24 months after the next one is released. A version pinned by default is how dated header versioning protects old scripts.

q: A pull request renames the response field amount to amountCents. All server tests pass. Which CI step stops it before it breaks the mobile app?
options: A unit test that compares the handler output with a snapshot
Running the OpenAPI linter on the new document only
Regenerating the TypeScript client in the server repository
A breaking-change diff of the OpenAPI document against main, such as oasdiff breaking --fail-on ERR
explain: Server tests were updated with the rename, so they pass; only a comparison with the previous contract sees that a field consumers rely on disappeared. A linter checks style rules within one document, and a snapshot updated in the same pull request records the new shape rather than protecting the old one.

q: Which pairing of use case and API style is the most defensible?
options: A public API for third-party developers in many languages: tRPC
High-volume calls between internal Go and Node services, some streaming: gRPC
A single React app and its Node backend in one TypeScript monorepo: gRPC
A partner API that must work with plain curl and HTTP caches: GraphQL
explain: gRPC fits internal, polyglot, high-volume and streaming calls with Protocol Buffers contracts. tRPC only serves TypeScript clients sharing the codebase, so it fails for a public API; a TypeScript monorepo is tRPC's home rather than gRPC's. curl and HTTP caching point to REST.

q: A webhook receiver verifies the HMAC like this, and every valid webhook is rejected. Why?
options: HMAC-SHA256 cannot be verified in Node without a native module
The secret must be passed as a string, not a Buffer
Re-serialising the parsed JSON changes the bytes, so the HMAC is computed over a different body
The receiver must answer 200 before verifying, or the sender times out
explain: The signature covers the exact bytes sent. Measured: {"a": 1,  "b":2} parsed and stringified came back as {"a":1,"b":2}, so the HMAC differs. Verify over the raw body (measured: a JSON content-type parser with parseAs: 'string', registered in an encapsulated Fastify plugin, gave the webhook route the raw string), then parse it. node:crypto computes HMAC-SHA256 natively.
